questions.q: What is the magnitude of $\vec{v} = (3, 4)$ (the page's default 2D vector)?
questions.explain: $|\vec{v}| = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{25} = 5$. Adding the components (7) or forgetting the square root (25) are common slips.

questions.q: The page's N-dimensional example is $(3, 4, 12)$. What is its magnitude?
questions.explain: $\sqrt{9 + 16 + 144} = \sqrt{169} = 13$ — the same Pythagorean rule, just with more squared terms.

questions.q: Why does the magnitude formula work in any number of dimensions?
options: It is the Pythagorean theorem applied repeatedly: add up all squared components, then take the square root
Because the magnitude is the average of the components
Because the magnitude is the largest component
It only works in 2D and 3D; higher dimensions need a different formula
questions.explain: $|\vec{v}| = \sqrt{v_1^2 + v_2^2 + \cdots + v_n^2}$ — the page calls it the Pythagorean theorem, supercharged for any number of dimensions.
